Qawwali is a form of Sufi devotional music from South Asia, most strongly associated with Pakistan but also performed in India and diaspora communities worldwide. Male singers, often performing in groups, lead audiences in ecstatic spiritual experiences through elaborate vocal improvisations, poetic devotional texts, and rhythmic hand-clapping. Qawwali represents the intersection of music, spirituality, and emotional intensity within Islamic mystical practice.

The word derives from an Arabic root meaning to speak or to say. Qawwals are professional singers of sacred poetry, traditionally attached to Sufi shrines and honored as spiritual intermediaries. Performances are centered on devotional poetry, often praising the Prophet Muhammad, Sufi saints, or God. Texts are repeated, elaborated, and varied across long performances that unfold over hours. The harmonium, a hand-pumped keyboard, and the tabla, a pair of drums, accompany the singers. The audience participates through hand-clapping and swaying, creating a collective spiritual trance state known as wajad.

Vocal technique emphasizes elaborate ornamentation, microtonal bending, and the ability to sustain notes while navigating complex emotional states. The style shares some features with Indian classical vocal traditions. Qawwali is traditionally performed at dargahs—Sufi shrines—during religious celebrations or weekly gatherings. Live performance is essential, as recorded versions are considered spiritually diminished. The tradition nearly disappeared in the mid-twentieth century due to modernization and religious conservatism, but was revived by legendary singers like Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, who brought qawwali to global audiences. UNESCO designated qawwali as Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in two thousand one.
